title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk

web_blocks.takeaway: Growth and margins are sound. The cash KPIs fail, and the working-capital days show why.

web_blocks.html: Operating KPIs are healthy. Revenue grew 32% in FY2026 on the snapshot and 28.6% in the first half of FY2027 [22]. The order book stood at about ₹6,500 crore at year-end FY2026 on management’s estimate, with ₹600 crore delivered in the year [1]. The Q3 FY2026 call described the book as over ₹6,500 crore [3]. Operating margin held at 37% for FY2026, and the Q4 EBITDA margin was 36.7% [5]. The Q4 FY2026 call transcript, as quoted on an aggregator page, reads: “delivering on our previously communicated top-line growth of approximately 25%+ for the current year” [6]. The record does not name the speaker, and no H1 FY2027 transcript was retrieved, so this is the latest guidance we hold.

The order-book history is only partly visible. In mid-2025 the energy order book was US$400 million, or about ₹3,400 crore [2]. The sources do not show that book updated by segment, so growth in the energy book since then cannot be measured. A broker citing a book of about ₹6,500 crore puts it at 11.5 times trailing revenue [34], or about 10.8 times FY2026 sales of ₹603 crore. That is an order-to-revenue ratio, and it shows how much future revenue is already committed if the book converts as expected. The order book is a management estimate, not an audited figure, and the record does not show its split by customer or by contract length.

The cash KPIs fail. Operating cash flow was negative ₹119 crore in FY2026 on the consolidated snapshot, and negative ₹45.8 crore in the first half of FY2027 [17]. Working-capital days rose to 304. Net debt of ₹423.8 crore equalled 1.6 times annualised EBITDA [18], a moderate leverage level, but leverage is rising while operating cash is negative, so part of the debt is funding working capital rather than capacity alone.

Management’s forward statements are the second test. The FY2028 run-rate target of above ₹13,000 million [36] is ₹1,300 crore a year. Against FY2026 sales of ₹603 crore, that is about 2.2 times in two years, or growth of roughly 47% a year. Growth at the guided 25% rate would give about ₹940 crore by FY2028. The gap between those two numbers is the claim the company is making. The sources do not explain how the difference will be produced beyond the capacity and qualification pipeline.

Capex is the third test, and it does not reconcile. Management planned ₹450 crore of FY2026 capex [12]. The consolidated snapshot shows an investing outflow of ₹71 crore for FY2026 and ₹918 crore for FY2025. Investing cash flow is net of any disposals or investments, so it need not equal capex. A ₹450 crore plan against a ₹71 crore net outflow is too large a gap to explain from the sources read, so this pass records it as unresolved rather than resolving it in management’s favour.

The moat KPIs change slowly. The company reports 1,700 qualified parts [28], wallet share of about 1 to 1.5% [38] and an export share of about 92% [31]. These are the least likely to move in a single year. Wallet share is the one that matters for growth, because it is the room to win without new facilities, and the sources do not show it moving.

Management’s language is consistently about delivery, visibility and capacity. The record gives its order-book and revenue statements a basis in the reported figures. It gives its cash-generation and capex statements little support, because the cash-flow figures are negative or do not reconcile. The fairest reading is that management has made the operating case well and has not yet shown the cash case. That is a reading about the record, not a judgment on the people.

On the record, management’s revenue statements have held so far. Revenue grew 32% in FY2026 [6], and the first half of FY2027 kept growing at about 29%. The guidance line does not name the year it covers, so the record cannot show that FY2026 beat it. Its cash statements have not held. Operating cash flow was negative in three of the last six years, including FY2026, the year of the strongest profit. Its capex statements do not reconcile with the cash-flow record in the sources read.

The use-of-funds statement is a checkable claim. The company reports that ₹621.8 crore of the ₹700 crore QIP has been deployed, with ₹78.2 crore retained [19]. Those amounts can be tested against the capex line in the next reported period. If the deployment shows up as fixed assets and capital work in progress, the statement holds. If it does not, the QIP funds are going somewhere other than the capacity the company describes.

Wallet share is also the structural-potential lever, and the arithmetic is simple. If the company’s share of customer spend in these categories rose from 1.5% to 2.0% with the same customer spend, revenue from those accounts would rise by about a third. Moving from 1.0% to 1.5% would add half. These are sensitivities on the reported range, not forecasts, and the sources do not show the company’s wallet share moving over time.

The quarterly growth record is the operating check on the annual guidance. Growth ran at 36.7%, 28.1%, 26.4% and 31.6% across the reported quarters [11][9][4][15]. Each is above the 25% guidance, so the growth KPI passes on every quarter with a reading. The first-half net profit growth of 6.6% [16] is the KPI that lagged, which is the sign that profit is not converting the revenue growth at the same rate.

The KPI scorecard has a clear split. The growth and margin readings are corroborated by the call and the snapshot. The moat readings rest on single sources, which limits how firmly they can be stated. The cash readings come from the consolidated snapshot and the standalone release, and the two agree in sign but differ in size. The capex reading does not reconcile at all. A reader should treat the first group as the basis for the business view and the second as the reason the verdict is conditional.

The dashboard also has blind spots. It carries no customer-level, segment-level or part-level line, so it cannot show whether growth comes from new parts, new customers or higher volume on existing parts. Each of those would mean something different for the moat and for the cash cycle, and the record does not separate them.

Three signals would change this reading: a full year of positive operating cash flow, falling working-capital days, and a segment profit split that appears in a later disclosure. Each would move the reading toward the bull case. Their absence keeps the cash watch in place, which is the basis for the KPI health reading in the business-quality file.
